stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many hydrologists have assumed that paving over land raises flood peaks in every kind of storm. A comparison of forty small catchments by hydrologist Ines Halvorsen complicates that view. During short, intense downpours, peak streamflow in heavily paved catchments was far higher than in unpaved ones. During long, soaking storms, however, unpaved soil quickly became saturated and shed water almost as fast as pavement did, so peak flows in the two kinds of catchment were nearly identical. If a region's climate shifted toward fewer short downpours and more prolonged rainfall, the difference in flood peaks between its paved and unpaved catchments would therefore ______
choices: likely shrink, since more of its storms would be the kind in which paving makes little difference to peak flow.
likely grow, since prolonged rainfall would send more total water off paved catchments than off unpaved ones.
likely shrink, since paved surfaces would begin absorbing rainfall nearly as well as saturated soil does.
likely grow, since short downpours are the storms in which paving most increases peak streamflow.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: short, intense storms → much higher peaks in paved catchments; long storms → almost no difference. The change in the question is fewer short storms and more long ones. That moves more of the region's storms into the 'almost no difference' category, so the gap between paved and unpaved catchments should shrink. Choice A gets both the direction and the reason right.

B.why: You brought in an idea the passage never states, that total runoff volume decides the gap. The study measured peak flow, and during long storms those peaks were nearly identical. More long storms means a smaller gap, not a bigger one.

C.why: You got the direction right but credited the change to the wrong surface. In the passage, the soil changes: it saturates and starts behaving like pavement. Nothing says pavement starts behaving like soil.

D.why: You remembered the right mechanism, that paving matters most in short downpours, but ran it backward. The question says those downpours become less common, so paving's effect shows up less often, which shrinks the gap instead of growing it.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: When the city of Marrow Falls required employers to offer paid sick leave, economists expected employee turnover to drop across the whole workforce. Labor economist Dario Okafor found a narrower effect. Turnover fell sharply among part-time hourly workers, most of whom had had no paid leave before the mandate. Among full-time salaried workers, nearly all of whom already received paid leave from their employers, turnover did not change measurably. Suppose a neighboring city with an almost entirely full-time salaried workforce, already widely covered by employer leave policies, adopted the same mandate. That city would most likely ______
choices: see little change in overall turnover, since the mandate mainly affected workers who had previously lacked paid leave.
see a sharp drop in turnover among its salaried workers, since the mandate sharply reduced turnover in Marrow Falls.
see turnover rise among its few part-time workers, since mandated leave makes those positions costlier to offer.
see a sharp drop in overall turnover, since the mandate's effect did not depend on which workers it reached.
explanation: The arrow is: mandate → lower turnover → only for workers who had no leave before. Already-covered salaried workers showed no change. The new city's workforce is almost entirely made up of that unaffected group, so the mandate should leave overall turnover there nearly unchanged.

B.why: You kept the direction, a drop in turnover, but attached it to the wrong group. In Marrow Falls, the sharp drop happened among part-time hourly workers. Salaried workers showed no measurable change.

C.why: You turned the direction around by adding a cost argument the passage never makes. The only evidence about part-time workers shows their turnover fell under the mandate.

D.why: The passage's main point is that the effect did depend on which workers the mandate reached. Assuming a uniform drop brings back the popular expectation that the study undercut.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Ornithologist Priya Venkataraman recorded marsh sparrows nesting near wind turbines, which emit a steady low-frequency hum. Males whose songs were naturally low-pitched raised the lowest notes of their songs, apparently so that the hum would not drown them out. Males whose songs were naturally high-pitched, and therefore already above the hum's range, did not change their songs. Venkataraman concluded that the shift was a direct response to the masking noise. If the turbines were replaced with models producing much less low-frequency hum, then ______
choices: males with low-pitched songs would likely lower their lowest notes, while high-pitched singers would change little.
males with high-pitched songs would likely lower their lowest notes, while low-pitched singers would change little.
males with low-pitched songs would likely raise their lowest notes, while high-pitched singers would change little.
males with either low- or high-pitched songs would likely lower their lowest notes by roughly equal amounts.
explanation: The arrow is: low-frequency hum → raised lowest notes → only in naturally low-pitched singers. If you remove most of the hum, the pressure that raised those notes goes away, so the low-pitched singers should drift back down. High-pitched singers never responded to the hum, so they should stay about the same.

B.why: You got the direction right but swapped the groups. The high-pitched singers never changed their songs, so there is nothing for them to undo. The low-pitched singers are the ones who shifted.

C.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Raising notes was the response to the hum. With the hum mostly gone, those birds have reason to come back down, not to rise further.

D.why: You applied the finding to every male even though the passage says only low-pitched singers responded to the noise. Nothing supports an equal change among high-pitched singers.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: It is often assumed that older adults gain the most from vaccine boosters simply because of their age. Immunologist Tomasz Reyes found otherwise. A booster sharply raised antibody levels in participants over 65 whose levels had waned substantially since their first dose, but older participants whose levels had stayed high gained only as modestly as younger participants did. The size of the gain tracked how far antibody levels had fallen before the booster, not the recipient's age. If older adults received the booster much sooner after their first dose, before much waning had occurred, their gain in antibody levels would likely ______
choices: be smaller than in the study, because their antibody levels would still be close to where they started.
be larger than in the study, because older adults respond more strongly to boosters than younger adults do.
be smaller than in the study, because younger adults would then gain more from the booster than older adults.
be larger than in the study, because an earlier booster leaves antibodies more time to keep accumulating.
explanation: The arrow is: more waning before the booster → bigger gain, regardless of age. Giving the booster earlier means less waning, so older adults would start from higher levels and see a smaller gain, just like the older participants whose levels had stayed high.

B.why: You went back to the popular view that the passage rejects. Reyes found that the gain depended on how much antibody levels had waned, not on age, so age alone can't produce a larger boost.

C.why: You got the direction right but moved the reasoning to a different group. The question asks about older adults' own gain compared with the study. How younger adults compare is beside the point and isn't established anyway.

D.why: You flipped the direction by adding a mechanism the passage never mentions. According to the study, an earlier booster means less waning, and less waning means a smaller gain.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Astronomers often estimate how quickly a galaxy forms stars by measuring its ultraviolet light, which young, massive stars emit in abundance. Interstellar dust, however, absorbs ultraviolet light, so in dusty galaxies much of that light never reaches telescopes, while in nearly dust-free galaxies almost all of it does. Radio emission linked to the same young stars passes through dust almost unimpeded. If a survey replaced its ultraviolet-based estimates with radio-based ones, the star formation rates it reports for the dustiest galaxies would likely ______
choices: rise substantially, while the rates it reports for nearly dust-free galaxies would change little.
fall substantially, while the rates it reports for nearly dust-free galaxies would change little.
change little, while the rates it reports for nearly dust-free galaxies would rise substantially.
rise substantially, and the rates it reports for nearly dust-free galaxies would rise by as much.
explanation: The arrow is: dust → lost ultraviolet light → star formation underestimated, mainly in dusty galaxies. Radio emission avoids that loss, so switching to it should push the dusty galaxies' estimates up. Dust-free galaxies lost almost no light to begin with, so their estimates should barely change.

B.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Dust hides ultraviolet light, so the old estimates for dusty galaxies were too low. Correcting them raises them.

C.why: You swapped the groups. Dust-free galaxies already delivered almost all their ultraviolet light, so their estimates were accurate. The dusty galaxies are the ones whose numbers would jump.

D.why: You stretched the correction to every galaxy. The passage says almost all ultraviolet light from dust-free galaxies reaches telescopes, so there is little for the switch to correct there.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Many cartographers assume that hillshading, the simulated shadows that make terrain look three-dimensional on a flat map, helps every reader understand the land. In a 2023 study, however, geographer Ilse Marten found that its benefit is narrower. Novice map readers given hillshaded maps chose correct hiking routes far more often than novices given otherwise identical unshaded maps. Experienced orienteers, by contrast, performed equally well with either version. Marten's findings suggest that if a park agency removed hillshading from its trail maps to cut printing costs, doing so would likely ______
choices: reduce route-finding accuracy among novice hikers while leaving experienced hikers' accuracy largely unchanged.
reduce route-finding accuracy among experienced hikers while leaving novice hikers' accuracy largely unchanged.
improve route-finding accuracy among novice hikers while leaving experienced hikers' accuracy largely unchanged.
reduce route-finding accuracy among novice and experienced hikers by roughly the same amount.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: hillshading → better route choices → novices only. Experienced orienteers did equally well with or without it. Removing hillshading reverses the condition, so the novices' advantage should disappear and their accuracy should fall. Experienced hikers never depended on the shading, so their accuracy should stay about the same. Only A gets both the direction (reduce) and the group (novices) right.

B.why: You got the direction right but swapped the groups. The passage says experienced orienteers performed equally well with or without hillshading, so removing it should not hurt them. It is the novices who relied on it.

C.why: You picked the right group but reversed the direction. Hillshading helped novices, so taking it away should lower their accuracy, not raise it.

D.why: This is the popular view the passage sets up to knock down: that hillshading helps everyone. Marten found that experienced orienteers were unaffected, so you have no grounds to expect an equal loss in both groups.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: When one state required employers to provide paid sick leave, economist Rafael Okonjo tracked how often workers left their jobs. Turnover among part-time workers fell sharply after the mandate took effect, while turnover among full-time workers stayed essentially flat. Okonjo attributes this split to a single factor: before the law, most full-time workers in the state already received paid sick leave, but few part-time workers did. If Okonjo is correct, a similar mandate adopted in a state where few full-time workers currently receive paid sick leave would likely ______
choices: reduce turnover among part-time workers but not among full-time workers.
reduce turnover among full-time workers as well as among part-time workers.
raise turnover among full-time workers while reducing it among part-time workers.
reduce turnover among full-time workers but not among part-time workers.
explanation: Write Okonjo's explanation as an arrow: newly gaining paid leave → lower turnover. Full-time workers in the first state showed no change only because they already had leave. In the new state, few full-time workers have leave, so they would be newly covered just as the part-time workers were. Both groups should therefore see turnover fall.

A.why: You copied the first state's result without applying the reason behind it. The full-time group was unaffected only because it was already covered. In the new state it isn't covered, so the explanation predicts that full-time workers would benefit too.

C.why: You reversed the direction for full-time workers. Nothing in the passage suggests that gaining paid leave makes anyone more likely to quit. The mechanism runs toward lower turnover.

D.why: You dropped the part-time group. Part-time workers lack paid leave in the new state as well, so by Okonjo's reasoning their turnover should also fall.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Dietary guidelines often present high-fiber diets as a reliable way to lower blood sugar. Nutrition scientist Hana Kovač found that the effect depends on the gut. Participants whose intestinal bacteria included the genus Prevotella showed a clear drop in fasting glucose after eight weeks on a high-fiber diet. Participants lacking Prevotella showed no measurable change. Kovač's results suggest that if a hospital added extra fiber to the meals of all its diabetic patients, the change would likely ______
choices: lower fasting glucose among patients whose gut bacteria include Prevotella but not among patients lacking it.
lower fasting glucose among patients lacking Prevotella but not among patients whose gut bacteria include it.
raise fasting glucose among patients whose gut bacteria include Prevotella but not among patients lacking it.
lower fasting glucose among all patients, though more among those whose gut bacteria include Prevotella.
explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: more fiber → lower fasting glucose → only in people with Prevotella. Participants without Prevotella showed no measurable change. A hospital-wide fiber increase applies that same condition to everyone, so you should expect a drop only among patients who carry Prevotella. Only A gets the direction (lower) and the group (Prevotella carriers) right.

B.why: You got the direction right but swapped the groups. The participants who lacked Prevotella were the ones who showed no change.

C.why: You picked the right group but reversed the direction. In Prevotella carriers, fiber lowered fasting glucose. It did not raise it.

D.why: This brings back the popular view that the passage undercuts. Participants without Prevotella showed no measurable change, so you can't claim that fiber lowers glucose for all patients, even by a smaller amount.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Radiocarbon dating measures when a plant or animal stopped absorbing carbon from the atmosphere. Charcoal from long-lived trees therefore poses a problem: a beam of oak may contain inner rings that formed centuries before the tree was felled and burned, so it can yield a date far older than the fire itself. Short-lived materials such as charred seeds avoid this flaw, because they formed within a year of being burned. A hearth that was first dated to 1200 BCE using oak charcoal, if redated using seeds from the same hearth, would likely ______
choices: yield a date later than 1200 BCE, indicating that the hearth was used more recently than first thought.
yield a date earlier than 1200 BCE, indicating that the hearth was used longer ago than first thought.
yield a date close to 1200 BCE, since seeds and charcoal both record when the hearth was in use.
yield a date later than 1200 BCE, indicating that the oak was felled more recently than first thought.
explanation: Write the flaw as an arrow: oak charcoal → date too old → for the fire. Seeds fix that flaw, so a seed date should be younger, meaning a later calendar date than 1200 BCE. That later date tells you about the fire, and so about when people used the hearth. Only A gets both the direction (later) and the thing being dated (the hearth's use) right.

B.why: You reversed the direction. The passage says oak charcoal makes dates too old, so correcting the error moves the date forward in time, not further back.

C.why: This ignores the flaw the passage spells out. Charcoal from old wood does not reliably record when the fire burned, which is exactly why seeds are described as the better material.

D.why: You got the direction right but attached it to the wrong thing. Seeds formed in the year of the fire, so they date the hearth's use. They say nothing about when the oak was cut.

stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
stimulus: Amateur astronomers in brightly lit cities often attach "nebula filters" to their telescopes, believing the filters improve views of every faint object. A survey led by astronomer Dalia Ferro found otherwise. The filters, which pass only the few wavelengths given off by glowing gas, made emission nebulae markedly easier to detect. They made galaxies, whose starlight spans a broad range of wavelengths, harder to detect. Ferro's results suggest that an observer who removed such a filter would likely find ______
choices: galaxies easier to detect and emission nebulae harder to detect.
emission nebulae easier to detect and galaxies harder to detect.
both galaxies and emission nebulae harder to detect than before.
galaxies easier to detect and emission nebulae no harder to detect.
explanation: Write the finding as two arrows. With the filter on: nebulae → easier to detect, galaxies → harder to detect. Removing the filter reverses both arrows, so galaxies should become easier to detect and nebulae harder. Only A flips both directions and keeps each one with the right kind of object.

B.why: This describes what the filter does when it's on, not what happens when it's removed. You read the finding correctly but didn't reverse it for the change the question names.

C.why: This follows the popular belief that the filter helps with every faint object, so taking it off must make everything worse. Ferro found that the filter actually hurt galaxy views, so removing it should help with galaxies.

D.why: You got the galaxies right but missed the nebulae. The filter made nebulae markedly easier to detect, so taking it away should make them harder to detect.
